chunks: Series versus parallel termination. The question: What is the difference between series and parallel termination?
Series and parallel termination both stop a signal from bouncing back along a line, but from opposite ends.
Series termination, a resistor at the driver, sends a half-height step down the line. The step doubles at the open far end, and the bounce dies when it returns to the source.
Parallel termination, a resistor at the far end, absorbs the full wave. Series wastes no steady power. Parallel gives a clean edge all along the line.
Think of a hallway with a hard wall at the far end. With series termination, you speak softly, the wall doubles the sound, and a curtain at your end soaks up the echo.
People mid-hall hear the soft voice first. With parallel termination, a curtain at the far wall absorbs everything, so everyone hears the full voice once.
That curtain costs steady effort (DC power).
The unterminated line (red) overshoots to 4. 7 volts (+43%) and rings with a period of 4 nanoseconds. Series termination (green) gives a clean step to the full 3.
3 volts one line delay after the edge launch. Parallel termination (orange) is equally clean but settles at 2. 36 volts because the driver and the resistor divide the supply.
Series (source) termination: a resistor at the driver so R out plus R s equals Z 0 ("Series vs parallel termination tradeoffs").
Parallel (load) termination: a resistor equal to Z 0 at the end of the line ("Source vs sink termination and matching").
Incident-wave switching: a receiver switching on the first wave that arrives, which receivers mid-line need.
V OH loss: the lower high level when a steady load pulls on the driver.
Take a 3. 3 volts driver with 20 ohms output impedance on a 50 ohms line. Unterminated, the first wave is 3. 3 times 50 over 70 equals 2. 36 volts, and it doubles to 4.
71 volts at the open end. With a 30 ohms series resistor, the first wave is 1. 65 volts and the far end steps cleanly to 3. 3 volts.
With 50 ohms to ground at the far end, the receiver sits at 2. 36 volts and the driver supplies 3. 3 over 70 about 47 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"Series termination puts a resistor at the driver so driver plus resistor equals Z0: the line gets a half-amplitude step, it doubles at the far end, and the reflection is absorbed at the source.
It costs no DC power, but only the end receiver sees a clean edge.
Parallel termination puts Z0 at the end of the line: the full step arrives and is absorbed, so any receiver along the line sees it cleanly, but the driver feeds a DC load and the high level drops.
Series for point-to-point and low power; parallel for multi-drop or when a clean wave along the line matters."
